key_points: Hash‑map solution: iterate once, for each number x check if target‑x exists in the map; if not, store x.
Time O(n), space O(n) for the map.
Edge cases: duplicate numbers, target equals twice a number, and empty input.

key_points: Classic sliding window with a hash set (or frequency map) to maintain unique characters.
Expand right pointer until a duplicate appears, then shrink left pointer to remove the duplicate.
Time: O(n) where n is string length; Space: O(min(m, n)) with m = size of character set.
Edge cases: empty string, all characters unique, all characters the same.
records.license: GPL-3.0 (source repository); problem links point to LeetCode

key_points: Two‑pointer technique: start with left at 0, right at end; compute area = (right‑left) * min(height[left], height[right]).
Move the pointer at the shorter line inward, because only a taller line could increase area.
Time: O(n) single pass; Space: O(1).
Edge cases: all heights equal, monotonic increasing or decreasing heights.
records.license: GPL-3.0 (source repository); problem links point to LeetCode

key_points: Sort the array, then fix one element and use two‑pointer scan for the remaining two to find triples summing to zero.
Time O(n^2) after O(n log n) sort; space O(1) extra (or O(n) if returning all triples).
Skip duplicates by advancing pointers past equal values; handle integer overflow by using long for sum if needed.
Edge cases: array length < 3, all zeros, and large magnitude numbers.
records.license: GPL-3.0 (source repository); problem links point to LeetCode

key_points: Compute a sorted character string or frequency signature for each word and use it as a hash key to group anagrams.
Overall O(N·K·log K) if sorting each word of length K, or O(N·K) with a 26‑length count array.
Space O(N·K) for the groups.
Edge cases: empty strings, words with same letters but different cases, and very long words.
records.license: GPL-3.0 (source repository); problem links point to LeetCode

key_points: First pass compute left products, second pass multiply by right products in output array.
Store result directly in output array to achieve O(1) extra space.
O(n) time, O(1) auxiliary space (output array excluded).
Correctly handles zeros and single‑element arrays.
records.license: GPL-3.0 (source repository); problem links point to LeetCode

key_points: Sort intervals by start time, then iterate merging overlapping intervals in O(n log n) time.
Maintain a result list; if current interval start ≤ last merged end, extend the end, else append new interval.
Time complexity: O(n log n) due to sorting; Space complexity: O(n) for the output (in‑place possible with O(1) extra).
Edge cases: empty input, single interval, fully overlapping intervals, intervals that just touch (end == start).
records.license: GPL-3.0 (source repository); problem links point to LeetCode

key_points: Use two pointers to expand a window until it contains all characters of the target (frequency map).
Then contract from the left to minimize window while still satisfying the requirement.
Time: O(N + M) where N is source length, M is target length; Space: O(K) for character counts (K = distinct chars).
Edge cases: target longer than source, characters not present, multiple minimal windows.
records.license: GPL-3.0 (source repository); problem links point to LeetCode

key_points: Two‑pointer technique on height array: maintain left/right indices, compute trapped water at the lower side, move that pointer inward.
Time O(n), space O(1).
Works for any non‑negative heights; if heights contain negatives, treat them as zero or reject input.
Edge cases: empty or single‑element array, monotonic increasing/decreasing heights, and large height values causing overflow.
records.license: GPL-3.0 (source repository); problem links point to LeetCode

key_points: Use two‑pointer or sliding‑window technique to locate each occurrence of the pattern and build the result string.
If the operation is "replace all occurrences of a substring with another", use StringBuilder to construct the output in O(n) time.
Time complexity O(n + m) where n is length of source and m length of pattern; space O(n) for the result.
Edge cases: overlapping patterns, empty pattern, pattern not found, replacement string longer than pattern.
records.license: GPL-3.0 (source repository); problem links point to LeetCode

records.text: Maximum Points You Can Obtain from Cards
key_points: Sort the card values; then use a sliding window of size k to compute the minimal difference between max and min in any window.
Algorithm: sort O(n log n), then for i from 0 to n‑k compute diff = cards[i+k‑1] – cards[i]; keep minimum.
Time O(n log n), space O(1) extra (or O(n) if sorting in‑place).
Edge cases: k == 0 or k > n (invalid), duplicate card values, already sorted input.
records.license: GPL-3.0 (source repository); problem links point to LeetCode

key_points: Dynamic programming with a hash map: dp[word] = 1 + max(dp[predecessor]) for all possible predecessors formed by removing one character.
Process words sorted by length so that all predecessors are computed before the word.
Time O(N · L²) where N is number of words and L average length (generating L possible predecessors per word); space O(N) for dp table.
Alternative: use a trie to reduce constant factors, but DP + hash map is the standard solution.
Edge cases: isolated words with no chain, duplicate words, very long words causing high L² cost.
records.license: GPL-3.0 (source repository); problem links point to LeetCode

key_points: Use a hash set to store all points for O(1) lookup.
Iterate over all pairs of points as potential diagonal corners; the other two corners are (x1, y2) and (x2, y1).
If both opposite corners exist, compute area = |x1‑x2| * |y1‑y2| and keep the minimum.
Time: O(N^2) where N is number of points; Space: O(N) for the set.
Edge cases: no rectangle possible → return 0; duplicate points are ignored by the set.
records.license: GPL-3.0 (source repository); problem links point to LeetCode

key_points: Maintain a map from x‑coordinate to a hash set of y‑coordinates for all added points.
When a query (x, y) arrives, iterate over all x' in the map where |x‑x'| == side length and check if y and y±side exist in both columns.
Count valid squares by checking the two possible y‑coordinates for each candidate column.
Add operation: O(1) average; Query: O(k) where k is number of columns at the required distance (worst‑case O(N)).
Space: O(N) for storing points; handle duplicate adds by using a multiset or counting occurrences.
records.license: GPL-3.0 (source repository); problem links point to LeetCode

records.text: Number of Unequal Triplets in Array
key_points: Count frequencies of each distinct value using a hash map.
Sort the unique values; then use three‑pointer or combinatorial formulas to count triples with all distinct values.
For each pair of distinct values (i, j) with i < j, the number of valid k is the count of values > j; accumulate using prefix sums.
Time: O(U log U) where U is number of unique values (or O(N log N) if sorting the whole array); Space: O(U).
Edge cases: fewer than three distinct numbers → answer 0; large frequencies handled by multiplication of counts.
records.license: GPL-3.0 (source repository); problem links point to LeetCode

key_points: Simulate water flow column by column using an array of heights.
For each unit of water, scan left from the drop point to find the first position with a lower height; if none, scan right; otherwise stay.
Implement the scan with two pointers moving outward until a lower height is found or bounds are reached.
Time: O(V * N) in worst case (V water units, N columns), acceptable for constraints up to ~10^4; Space: O(N) for heights.
Edge cases: flat terrain where water piles up; boundaries where water spills over the ends.
records.license: GPL-3.0 (source repository); problem links point to LeetCode

key_points: The optimal meeting point on a grid is the median of the x‑coordinates and the median of the y‑coordinates of all people.
Collect all row indices and column indices separately, sort them, and pick the middle element (or any median for even count).
Sum of Manhattan distances to the median gives minimal total distance.
Time: O(N log N) for sorting (N = number of people); Space: O(N) for the coordinate lists.
Edge cases: multiple optimal points when even number of people – any median works.
records.license: GPL-3.0 (source repository); problem links point to LeetCode

key_points: Use a stack to process the encoded string character by character.
When encountering a digit, parse the full number and push it onto a count stack; push a marker for '['.
When ']' is found, pop characters until the marker, repeat the substring count times, and push the result back onto the character stack.
Finally, join the stack to produce the decoded string.
Time: O(L) where L is length of the output string; Space: O(L) for the stack.
records.license: GPL-3.0 (source repository); problem links point to LeetCode

key_points: Sort the citation counts (or use counting sort for O(n) when citations are bounded).
Iterate from highest to lowest to find the largest h where at least h papers have ≥ h citations.
Time: O(n log n) with sorting (or O(n) with counting sort); Space: O(1) extra (or O(n) for count array).
Edge cases: empty list, all citations zero, or all citations large enough for h = n.
records.license: GPL-3.0 (source repository); problem links point to LeetCode

records.text: Amount of New Area Painted Each Day
key_points: Model each day as a union‑find (DSU) of painted cells; when a new cell is painted, union it with already painted neighbours.
Maintain the size of each connected component; the newly painted area contributed by the day is the size of the component after unions minus the sum of sizes before unions.
Process days in order, performing up to 4 union operations per cell.
Time: O(D α(N)) where D is number of days (cells) and α is inverse Ackermann; Space: O(N) for DSU arrays.
Edge cases: painting isolated cells (component size 1) and painting cells that merge multiple existing components.
records.license: GPL-3.0 (source repository); problem links point to LeetCode

key_points: Use in‑place bucket sort: iterate through array and place each positive integer x (1 ≤ x ≤ n) at index x‑1 by swapping.
After placement, scan from left; first index i where nums[i] ≠ i+1 gives answer i+1; if all correct, answer is n+1.
Time O(n) – each element swapped at most once; Space O(1) extra.
Edge cases: empty array → 1; all negatives or zeros → 1; array containing 1..n → n+1.
records.license: GPL-3.0 (source repository); problem links point to LeetCode

key_points: Greedy linear scan keeping the farthest reachable index (maxReach).
For each index i ≤ maxReach, update maxReach = max(maxReach, i + nums[i]); if maxReach reaches or exceeds last index, return true.
If i exceeds maxReach before the end, return false.
Time O(N), space O(1).
Edge cases: first element 0 with length >1 (immediate false), large jumps, single‑element array.
records.license: GPL-3.0 (source repository); problem links point to LeetCode

key_points: Apply DFS or BFS to explore each connected component of '1's, marking visited cells to avoid recounting.
Iterate the grid; when a '1' is found, increment island count and launch a flood fill to mark the whole island.
Time complexity O(m·n) for an m×n grid; space complexity O(m·n) in worst case for recursion stack or explicit queue.
Edge cases: empty grid, single‑cell grid, all water, all land, and grids with diagonal adjacency (which should be ignored).
Can also use Union‑Find: union neighboring lands, then count distinct roots; same O(m·n) time, O(m·n) space.
records.license: GPL-3.0 (source repository); problem links point to LeetCode

key_points: Model courses as a directed graph where nodes are courses and edges are prerequisites.
Use Kahn's algorithm (BFS topological sort) or DFS with cycle detection to produce a valid ordering.
Maintain an indegree array; repeatedly enqueue nodes with indegree zero.
Time complexity O(V + E) and space O(V + E) for adjacency list and indegree storage.
Edge cases: disconnected components, multiple valid orders, and detection of cycles (return empty list).
records.license: GPL-3.0 (source repository); problem links point to LeetCode

key_points: Perform an in‑order traversal while keeping track of the previous node value.
At each node, verify that current value > previous value; also propagate min/max bounds recursively.
Recursive solution: helper(node, low, high) returns false if node.val not in (low, high) or subtrees violate BST property.
Time: O(N) for visiting each node once; Space: O(H) recursion stack where H is tree height.
Edge cases: duplicate values (must be rejected), extreme integer limits, and skewed trees causing O(N) stack depth.
records.license: GPL-3.0 (source repository); problem links point to LeetCode

key_points: Use post‑order DFS returning two values: max gain from left/right sub‑paths and the best path sum seen so far.
For each node, compute maxSingle = node.val + max(0, leftGain, rightGain); maxTop = node.val + max(0, leftGain) + max(0, rightGain).
Update global answer with maxTop; return maxSingle to parent.
Time: O(N) traversing each node once; Space: O(H) recursion stack.
Edge cases: all negative values (answer is the largest single node), and large depth causing stack overflow – can be converted to iterative.
records.license: GPL-3.0 (source repository); problem links point to LeetCode

key_points: Bidirectional BFS between beginWord and endWord to reduce search space.
At each level, generate all one‑letter transformations; only keep those present in the word list.
Time: O(N·L·26) where N = number of words, L = word length; Space: O(N) for visited sets.
Edge cases: beginWord not in list, no possible transformation, start equals end.
records.license: GPL-3.0 (source repository); problem links point to LeetCode

key_points: Use DFS or BFS to traverse the graph, cloning each node on first visit and storing the mapping original→clone in a hash map.
When visiting a node, create its clone (if not already created) and recursively/iteratively clone all its neighbors, linking them via the cloned neighbor list.
Time complexity O(V+E) because each node and edge is processed once; space complexity O(V) for the visited map and recursion/queue stack.
Handle self‑loops and multiple edges correctly by checking the map before creating a new clone.
Return the clone of the input node; if the input is null, return null.
records.license: GPL-3.0 (source repository); problem links point to LeetCode

key_points: Choose a deterministic representation – e.g., preorder traversal with sentinel (e.g., "#") for null nodes.
Serialize: DFS preorder, appending node values and sentinel separated by commas; Deserialize: read tokens recursively rebuilding the tree.
Both operations run in O(N) time and O(N) space for the output string / recursion stack.
Edge cases: empty tree (produces just sentinel), trees with only left or only right children, and large depth requiring tail‑recursion or iterative stack to avoid overflow.
records.license: GPL-3.0 (source repository); problem links point to LeetCode

key_points: Model accounts as nodes in a Union‑Find (Disjoint Set Union) structure; each email is a node and accounts share emails → union their sets.
First map each email to an account index, performing union operations for all emails within the same account.
After unions, group emails by their root parent, sort each group, and prepend the account name (taken from the original account).
Time complexity O(A·α(N)) ≈ O(A) where A is total number of emails; sorting each group adds O(A log A) overall. Space O(A) for maps and DSU arrays.
Edge cases: accounts with no emails, duplicate emails across many accounts, and handling of case‑sensitive email strings.
records.license: GPL-3.0 (source repository); problem links point to LeetCode

key_points: Treat each equation a / b = k as a weighted edge a→b with weight k; the graph is a set of connected components.
Answer queries by finding a path between numerator and denominator and multiplying edge weights; use Union‑Find with weight ratios or DFS/BFS per query.
Union‑Find with path compression stores relative ratios, giving near O(α(N)) per union/find; total O(N + Q·α(N)). DFS approach is O(N+Q·E).
Edge cases: variables that never appear, division by zero not present by problem guarantee, and disconnected components returning -1.0.
records.license: GPL-3.0 (source repository); problem links point to LeetCode

key_points: Model the alien alphabet as a directed graph where an edge u→v means u comes before v, derived from the first differing character of consecutive words.
Perform topological sort (Kahn's BFS or DFS) to produce a valid ordering; detect cycles to return empty or error.
Time O(C+U) where C is total characters in all words and U is number of unique letters; Space O(U+E) for graph structures.
Edge cases: prefix situation (e.g., "abc" before "ab" → invalid), isolated letters with no edges, and multiple valid orders (any topological order is acceptable).
records.license: GPL-3.0 (source repository); problem links point to LeetCode

records.text: The Earliest Moment When Everyone Become Friends
key_points: Sort the friendship logs by timestamp.
Use a Union‑Find (DSU) to merge friend groups; after each union, check if the size of the component containing all members equals N.
The first timestamp when the component size reaches N is the answer.
Time: O(M log M) for sorting M logs plus near‑constant DSU ops; Space: O(N) for DSU arrays.
Edge cases: disconnected graph (return -1); multiple logs with same timestamp – process all before checking.
records.license: GPL-3.0 (source repository); problem links point to LeetCode

records.text: Checking Existence of Edge Length Limited Paths
key_points: Sort both edge list and queries by the limit value.
Use a DSU to add edges whose length ≤ current query limit; after adding, check if the two query nodes are connected.
Store answers in original order after processing all queries.
Time: O((E+Q) α(N)) after sorting O(E log E + Q log Q); Space: O(N) for DSU.
Edge cases: queries with limit smaller than any edge (answer false); self‑queries (always true).
records.license: GPL-3.0 (source repository); problem links point to LeetCode

records.text: Step-By-Step Directions From a Binary Tree Node to Another
key_points: Find the lowest common ancestor (LCA) of the start and destination nodes using parent pointers or a DFS map.
From start node, move up to LCA recording 'U' moves; from LCA, move down to destination recording 'L' or 'R' based on child direction.
Combine the upward and downward strings to form the full path.
Time: O(H) where H is tree height for both LCA search and path construction; Space: O(H) for recursion or stacks.
Edge cases: start equals destination (empty string); one node is ancestor of the other (no upward moves or no downward moves).
records.license: GPL-3.0 (source repository); problem links point to LeetCode

key_points: Model the grid as a graph where each cell is a node connected to its four neighbors.
Use Dijkstra's algorithm (or a min‑heap BFS) where the cost of a path is the maximum elevation seen so far; the answer is the minimum possible maximum.
Initialize the heap with the start cell (0,0) and its elevation, repeatedly pop the smallest‑cost node and update neighbors with max(currentCost, neighborElevation).
Time complexity O(N log N) for N = rows × cols; space O(N) for the heap and visited set.
Edge cases: single‑cell grid, grids with equal elevations, and handling out‑of‑bounds neighbors.
records.license: GPL-3.0 (source repository); problem links point to LeetCode

key_points: Treat each cell as a node; the effort of an edge is the absolute height difference between adjacent cells.
Find a path minimizing the maximum edge weight – classic "minimax" path solved with binary search + BFS/DFS or with Dijkstra using max‑edge as path cost.
Binary‑search approach: search effort value E, run BFS only through edges ≤ E; O(log C·M·N) where C is height range.
Dijkstra approach: priority queue keyed by current path's max edge, yielding O(M·N log(M·N)).
Edge cases: start equals end, uniform heights, and large height differences requiring full binary‑search range.
records.license: GPL-3.0 (source repository); problem links point to LeetCode

key_points: Perform a post‑order DFS; a node is a leaf if both its left and right children are null after recursion.
Collect node values in a list when they satisfy the leaf condition, then return the list.
Time complexity O(N) where N is number of nodes; space O(H) recursion stack (H = tree height).
Edge cases: empty tree (return empty list) and trees where all nodes are leaves (single‑node tree).
records.license: GPL-3.0 (source repository); problem links point to LeetCode

key_points: A cell can flow to the Pacific if it can reach any cell on the top or left border, and to the Atlantic if it can reach any cell on the bottom or right border.
Run two DFS/BFS traversals starting from all Pacific border cells and all Atlantic border cells, moving only to neighbors with height ≥ current (reverse flow).
Intersection of the two visited sets gives cells that can reach both oceans.
Time complexity O(M·N) for each of the two traversals; total O(M·N). Space O(M·N) for visited matrices and recursion/queue.
Edge cases: single row or column grids, and equal‑height plateaus that allow water to spread widely.
records.license: GPL-3.0 (source repository); problem links point to LeetCode

key_points: Insert all dictionary words into a Trie to enable prefix checks.
Traverse the Trie depth‑first, building candidate words; keep the longest word that is also a valid prefix chain (each prefix exists in the set).
When multiple words share length, choose lexicographically smallest (handled by traversing children in alphabetical order).
Time complexity O(ΣL) where ΣL is total characters in all words; space O(ΣL) for the Trie.
Edge cases: empty dictionary, words with no valid prefix chain, and ties on length.
records.license: GPL-3.0 (source repository); problem links point to LeetCode

records.text: Delete Leaves With a Given Value
key_points: Use a post‑order DFS; after processing children, if a node's value equals the target and both children are null (or have been deleted), delete the node by returning null to its parent.
Return the possibly updated root after recursion.
Time complexity O(N) for N nodes; space O(H) recursion stack.
Edge cases: deleting leaves at the root (entire tree becomes null), multiple consecutive deletions causing parent to become a leaf, and empty tree.
records.license: GPL-3.0 (source repository); problem links point to LeetCode

key_points: Dynamic programming: dp[i] = minimum coins needed to make amount i; initialize dp[0]=0 and others to INF.
Iterate amounts from 1..target and for each coin update dp[i] = min(dp[i], dp[i‑coin]+1).
Time complexity O(N·M) where N is number of coin types and M is the amount; space O(M).
If dp[amount] stays INF, return -1 (no solution).
Edge cases: amount = 0 (return 0), coin values larger than amount, duplicate coin denominations.
records.license: GPL-3.0 (source repository); problem links point to LeetCode

key_points: Dynamic programming: dp[i][j] = min edits to convert first i chars of word1 to first j chars of word2.
Recurrence: if chars equal dp[i][j]=dp[i-1][j-1]; else dp[i][j]=1+min(dp[i-1][j] (delete), dp[i][j-1] (insert), dp[i-1][j-1] (replace)).
Initialize first row/column with i/j (cost of all inserts/deletes). Time O(m n), space O(m n) or O(min(m,n)) with rolling arrays.
Handle empty strings, Unicode characters, and large lengths by optimizing space.
Result is dp[m][n]; can also reconstruct edit sequence if needed.
records.license: GPL-3.0 (source repository); problem links point to LeetCode

key_points: Expand Around Center: for each index treat it as a center of odd and even length palindrome and expand while characters match.
Track longest palindrome start and length during expansion.
Time complexity: O(n²) worst case; Space complexity: O(1).
Manacher's algorithm can achieve O(n) time with O(n) extra space if optimal solution is required.
Edge cases: all identical characters, empty string, single character string.
records.license: GPL-3.0 (source repository); problem links point to LeetCode

key_points: Classic DP O(n²) solution: dp[i] = 1 + max(dp[j]) for all j < i with nums[j] < nums[i].
Patience‑sorting / binary‑search method gives O(n log n) by maintaining tails array.
Space: O(n) for dp array or tails array.
Edge cases: strictly decreasing sequence (LIS length 1), all equal elements, empty array.
records.license: GPL-3.0 (source repository); problem links point to LeetCode

records.text: Longest Increasing Path in a Matrix
key_points: Dynamic programming with memoization on each cell: longestIncreasingPath(i,j) = 1 + max of neighbors with higher value.
DFS with caching avoids recomputation; each cell is processed once.
Time complexity O(M·N) because each cell's DFS explores at most four neighbors once; space O(M·N) for memo table plus O(H) recursion stack.
Edge cases: matrix with all equal values (answer 1), single‑row/column matrices, and large monotonic gradients.
records.license: GPL-3.0 (source repository); problem links point to LeetCode

key_points: Dynamic programming on intervals: dp[l][r] = max coins obtainable by bursting balloons in (l, r) exclusive.
Treat virtual balloons with value 1 at both ends; for each possible last burst k in (l, r), dp[l][r] = max(dp[l][k] + dp[k][r] + nums[l]*nums[k]*nums[r]).
Fill dp by increasing interval length; time O(N³), space O(N²).
Edge cases: empty input (return 0), single balloon, handling the added 1s correctly.
Optimization: use bottom‑up loops; no better than O(N³) known for this problem.
records.license: GPL-3.0 (source repository); problem links point to LeetCode

key_points: Binary search the answer: the minimal possible largest subarray sum lies between max(nums) and sum(nums).
For a candidate mid, greedily partition the array counting how many subarrays are needed with sum ≤ mid; if count ≤ k, mid is feasible.
Binary search converges in O(log S) where S = sum(nums)‑max(nums); each feasibility check is O(N).
Overall time O(N log S), space O(1).
Edge cases: k = 1 (answer = total sum), k = length of array (answer = max element), and arrays with large numbers causing overflow (use 64‑bit).
records.license: GPL-3.0 (source repository); problem links point to LeetCode

records.text: Longest Arithmetic Subsequence of Given Difference
key_points: Transform the problem to a longest subsequence where each element equals previous + diff.
Use a hash map dp where dp[x] = length of longest subsequence ending with value x; update dp[num] = dp.get(num‑diff, 0) + 1 while iterating.
Time complexity O(N) for N numbers; space O(N) for the map.
Handle negative diff and duplicate numbers correctly because map stores best length per value.
Edge cases: empty array, diff = 0 (count repetitions), and large integer values requiring 64‑bit keys.
records.license: GPL-3.0 (source repository); problem links point to LeetCode

records.text: Maximum Number of Points with Cost
key_points: Model points as nodes on a line; moving from i to j costs |i‑j| plus a given cost array value at j.
Use DP with a monotonic queue or segment tree to compute dp[i] = max(dp[j] + cost[i] - |i‑j|) efficiently.
Two‑pass solution: left‑to‑right maintains max(dp[j] + j) and right‑to‑left maintains max(dp[j] - j), giving O(N) time.
Overall time O(N), space O(N) for dp (or O(1) extra if updating in place).
Edge cases: single point, all costs negative (choose not to move), and large N requiring 64‑bit arithmetic.
records.license: GPL-3.0 (source repository); problem links point to LeetCode

records.text: Count Square Submatrices with All Ones
key_points: DP where dp[i][j] stores size of largest square ending at (i,j); dp[i][j] = 1 + min(dp[i‑1][j], dp[i][j‑1], dp[i‑1][j‑1]) if matrix[i][j] == 1.
Sum all dp values to get total count of all‑ones squares.
Time complexity O(M·N); space can be O(N) by keeping only previous row.
Edge cases: first row/column (dp = matrix value), all zeros (answer 0), and all ones (triangular number of squares).
records.license: GPL-3.0 (source repository); problem links point to LeetCode

key_points: Binary search with pivot logic: compare nums[mid] with nums[right] to identify sorted side.
Check if target lies in the sorted half; adjust left/right accordingly.
Time: O(log n) for distinct elements; Space: O(1) iterative.
Edge cases: array of size 1, target not present, and handling of duplicates (may degrade to O(n)).

key_points: Binary search on eating speed K (1 … maxPile). For each K, compute total hours = Σ ceil(pile/K); if hours ≤ H, K is feasible.
Check feasibility in O(n) time; binary search adds O(log maxPile) factor → O(n log maxPile).
Space O(1) extra.
Edge cases: H equals number of piles (must eat each pile in one hour → K = maxPile), H much larger than total bananas (K = 1), and integer overflow when summing hours.
Implementation tip: use integer division (pile + K - 1) / K to compute ceil without floating point.

key_points: Binary‑search partition method: partition both arrays so that left halves contain half of total elements.

During a left‑to‑right sweep, for each prefix sum query the BST for the number of earlier sums within the target range and then insert the current sum.

records.text: Restaurant waitlist data structure. Description: addGroup, group leaves anytime, seat best group for a table size by arrival order + size.
key_points: Maintain a doubly‑linked list (or ordered queue) of groups in arrival order, each node storing group size and a pointer to the next larger‑or‑equal size group.
When seating a table of size S, scan the list from the front until you find the first group with size ≤ S; remove that node and return it.
addGroup appends to the tail in O(1); group leaves (by reference) removes its node in O(1) using the stored pointer.
Overall operations are O(1) for insertion/removal and O(g) worst‑case for seating, where g is number of waiting groups; can be improved to O(log g) with a balanced BST keyed by (arrivalIndex, size).
Edge cases: no group fits the table (return null), groups of size zero, and groups leaving before being seated.

records.text: Number of lakes on an island. Description: Grid of water/land; given one land coordinate, count enclosed lakes (flood-fill variant).
key_points: Treat the given land cell as a seed and perform a flood‑fill (DFS/BFS) over 4‑directional neighbours that are water.
Mark visited water cells; count each connected component of water that is completely surrounded by land (i.e., never reaches the grid border).
Implementation: start from the seed, explore all reachable water; if any visited water touches the border, the component is not a lake.
Time complexity O(m × n) for an m×n grid; space O(m × n) for the visited matrix or recursion stack.
Edge cases: the seed is on land (answer 0), grid of all water, and narrow corridors that connect water to the border.

records.text: Root an undirected acyclic graph as a binary tree. Description: Nodes have <=3 edges; find a node that, when rooted, yields a valid binary tree.
key_points: Because the graph is acyclic and each node has degree ≤ 3, a valid binary‑tree rooting requires that every node have at most two children after removing the parent edge.
Try each node as a candidate root: perform a DFS, treating the incoming edge as the parent, and verify that every visited node has ≤ 2 unvisited neighbours (children).
If a node satisfies the condition for the whole component, it can be the root; otherwise no such root exists.
Time complexity O(V + E) per candidate, but can be reduced to O(V + E) total by a single DFS that records the number of “extra” children needed and propagating constraints upward.
Edge cases: isolated node (trivially a root), a chain (any endpoint works), and a node of degree 3 (must be the root).

records.text: Alternating-color tree root. Description: Graph nodes colored black/white; choose root so colors alternate per layer.
key_points: Root must be chosen so that the bipartite coloring of the graph matches the required alternating layers: all nodes at even depth share one color, odd depth the other.
Perform a BFS from a candidate root, checking that each edge connects nodes of opposite colors; this is exactly the condition for the graph to be bipartite with the root’s color fixed.
If the graph is bipartite, any node of one color can serve as a root for an alternating‑color tree; otherwise no such root exists.
Time complexity O(V + E) for the BFS; space O(V) for visited/color arrays.
Edge cases: disconnected components (must be handled separately), single‑node graph (trivially valid), and graphs with odd cycles (fail).

records.text: Top-K most talkative users. Description: Parse chat-log files at given paths, return K users by word count.
key_points: Stream each chat‑log file line by line, split on whitespace to count words per user, and maintain a hash map {user → totalWordCount}.
Use a min‑heap of size K to keep the top‑K users: for each user update the map, then push (count, user) onto the heap and pop when size exceeds K.
After processing all files, extract the heap contents and sort descending to return the K most talkative users.
Time complexity O(T + U log K) where T is total number of words and U the number of distinct users; space O(U + K).
Edge cases: ties in word count (define tie‑break rule), empty files, and users with zero words.

records.text: Network of teleporters. Description: Graph reachability over teleporter nodes/connections.
key_points: Model teleporters as directed edges; reachability reduces to a graph traversal (DFS/BFS) from the start node.
If teleporters can be used repeatedly, compute the transitive closure using Floyd‑Warshall (O(N³)) for small N or repeated BFS/DFS for each query (O(N + E) per query).

For many queries, pre‑process with strongly connected components (Tarjan/Kosaraju) and build a DAG of SCCs; then answer reachability by checking ancestor‑descendant relationship in the DAG (e.g., via topological order and bitsets).
Time/space trade‑off: O(N + E) preprocessing + O(1) per query with bitset reachability, or O(N + E) per query with plain BFS.
Edge cases: isolated teleporters, self‑loops, and disconnected components.

records.text: Car rental bookings overlap. Description: Batch of pickup/return times; find peak concurrent bookings.
key_points: Treat each booking as an interval [pickup, return). Create two event lists: one for pickups (+1) and one for returns (‑1).
Sort all events by time (break ties by processing returns before pickups to avoid counting back‑to‑back bookings as overlapping).
Sweep through the sorted events, maintaining a running count of active bookings; the maximum count encountered is the peak concurrency.
Time complexity O(N log N) for N bookings due to sorting; space O(N) for the event list.
Edge cases: bookings with identical start/end times, zero‑length bookings, and bookings that span midnight (if times are not normalized).

records.text: Guess-the-word sequence validation. Description: Decide if guessed sequences produce a valid ordering (topological sort / cycle detection).
key_points: Model each guess as a directed edge A → B meaning A must appear before B; the problem becomes checking if the resulting graph is a DAG.
Build the graph from the sequence, then run a cycle detection algorithm (DFS with recursion stack or Kahn’s topological sort).
If a topological ordering exists, the guess sequence is valid; otherwise a cycle indicates contradictory ordering.
Time complexity O(V + E) where V is number of distinct words and E the number of guess relations; space O(V + E).
Edge cases: repeated guesses (duplicate edges), isolated words (no constraints), and self‑referencing guesses (immediate cycle).

records.text: Coin collection on a board. Description: Grid DP / simulation.
key_points: Define dp[i][j] as the maximum coins collectable when reaching cell (i, j); transition from the allowed predecessor cells (e.g., up/left depending on movement rules).
Initialize dp at the start cell with its coin value; fill the table row‑by‑row or column‑by‑column using dp[i][j] = coin[i][j] + max(dp[prev]).

If moves are unrestricted (four directions) and cycles are possible, use Dijkstra/priority‑queue on a weighted graph where each cell is a node and edge weight is negative coin value to find max‑gain path.
Time complexity O(m × n) for simple monotone moves; O(m × n log (mn)) if using Dijkstra for arbitrary moves.
Edge cases: cells with negative coins, unreachable cells, and board boundaries.

Expose operations such as insert(text), delete(k), moveCursor(pos), and getText() to mimic a typical text editor.
Discuss language‑specific considerations: Unicode handling, immutable strings vs mutable buffers, and thread‑safety if required.

records.text: URL router with placeholder patterns. Description: processHandler registers patterns such as /users/{userId}/photo/{photoId}; getHandler takes a concrete path and returns the matching pattern. Trie with literal and placeholder children, precedence when both match, follow-ups on wildcards, HTTP methods and concurrent registration.
key_points: Use a trie where each node has a map for literal segments and a special child for a placeholder (e.g., "{*}")
When matching a concrete path, try the literal child first; if it fails, fall back to the placeholder child to satisfy precedence rules
Store the full pattern string at leaf nodes; on a match return that stored pattern
Time complexity: O(L) per registration or lookup, where L is the number of '/'‑separated segments; space O(T) for total nodes in the trie
Edge cases: duplicate patterns, trailing slashes, multiple placeholders in a row, and handling HTTP method as an extra dimension (store a method‑to‑pattern map at leaf)

records.text: Timed-out RPC calls from paired log records. Description: Start and end records arrive in time order with a timeout; return calls whose duration exceeds it, measure open calls against the last timestamp, sort by start time then call id.
key_points: Maintain a hash map from call‑id to its start timestamp when a "start" record arrives
When an "end" record arrives, compute duration = end‑time – start‑time; if duration > timeout, add the call‑id to the result list
After processing all records, for any call still open, treat the last observed timestamp as its end time and apply the same timeout check
Complexities: O(N) time for N log entries, O(M) space for M concurrent calls (hash map)
Edge cases: missing start or end records, zero‑length windows, timeout equal to duration, and large timestamps requiring 64‑bit arithmetic

records.text: Dependency-safe deletion order. Description: parents[] gives a forest, plus extra [a before b] constraints; return the lexicographically smallest child-before-parent order, or an empty list on a cycle (topological sort with a min-heap).
key_points: Model the forest and extra constraints as a directed graph; edges point from a node that must appear before another
Perform a topological sort using a min‑heap (priority queue) to always pick the smallest available node, guaranteeing lexicographically smallest order
If at any step the heap is empty while nodes remain, a cycle exists → return empty list
Time complexity: O(V + E + V log V) (heap operations), space O(V + E)
Edge cases: multiple roots, duplicate constraints, self‑loops, and large fan‑out requiring efficient adjacency storage

records.text: Trimmed sliding-window means. Description: For each window of fixed size drop the k largest values by multiplicity and return the mean of the rest as a reduced fraction; two balanced heaps or an ordered multiset.
key_points: Maintain two balanced multisets (or two heaps with lazy deletion): a max‑heap for the k largest elements and a min‑heap for the rest
When the sliding window moves, insert the new value, rebalance so the max‑heap holds exactly k elements, then remove the outgoing value with lazy deletion
The sum of the elements in the min‑heap gives the numerator; denominator = windowSize – k; reduce the fraction with gcd
Overall O(N log W) time where W is window size, O(W) space for the two heaps
Edge cases: k = 0 (no removal), k ≥ windowSize (mean undefined → treat as 0 or skip), duplicate values, and integer overflow when summing

records.text: Group courses into earliest possible rounds. Description: Round 1 has no prerequisites, a course goes in round r+1 where r is its latest prerequisite's round; nested lists sorted within rounds, empty on a cycle (Parallel Courses variant).
key_points: Treat courses as nodes in a DAG; edges go from prerequisite → dependent course

Compute indegrees and perform a BFS (Kahn’s algorithm) level‑by‑level: all nodes with indegree 0 belong to round 1, then decrement indegrees of their neighbors and collect the next batch for round 2, etc.
Collect nodes of each round into a list and sort each list to satisfy the “nested lists sorted within rounds” requirement
If after processing there are still nodes with non‑zero indegree, a cycle exists → return empty list
Complexities: O(N + E) time, O(N + E) space; edge cases include isolated courses, multiple independent prerequisite chains, and self‑dependency

records.text: Deduplicate and order batch and streaming logs. Description: Deterministic dedup under first-seen and latest-seen policies; late events, stale versions, state expiry, up to 200k operations.
key_points: Use a hash map from log‑id to a struct holding the latest timestamp and the payload; for first‑seen policy keep the earliest timestamp, for latest‑seen keep the greatest
When a new event arrives, compare its timestamp with the stored one; update or ignore according to the chosen policy, and optionally evict entries older than a TTL to enforce state expiry
Both batch and streaming modes share the same deduplication logic; the streaming version processes events incrementally while the batch version can sort by timestamp first if needed
Time complexity: O(N) for N events; space O(U) for U unique log‑ids currently retained (bounded by 200 k)
Edge cases: out‑of‑order timestamps, duplicate events with identical timestamps, TTL expiration causing re‑insertion, and handling of null or malformed payloads

records.text: Connected clusters of 2D points. Description: Points within a radius are linked, transitively; duplicate coordinates, exact integer distance comparison, overflow safety; Union-Find.
key_points: Model each point as a node; connect two nodes with an edge if the Euclidean distance ≤ radius (compare squared distances to avoid floating‑point errors and overflow with 64‑bit integers)
Run Union‑Find (Disjoint Set Union) over all pairs; for each pair within radius, union their sets
After processing, the number of distinct clusters equals the number of unique root representatives

Time complexity: O(P α(P)) where P is number of points (α is inverse Ackermann); building all candidate pairs can be optimized with spatial hashing or kd‑tree if P is large, otherwise O(P²) brute force
Edge cases: duplicate coordinates (distance = 0 → same cluster), radius = 0, integer overflow when computing (dx*dx + dy*dy), and negative coordinates

records.text: Prefix-matching simple paths in a labeled graph. Description: Count simple paths whose labels spell every nonempty prefix of a query word; paths start anywhere and never revisit a vertex; DFS with pruning.
key_points: Perform a DFS from every vertex, carrying the current prefix index; at each step, if the edge label matches the next character of the query, continue the path
Count a path whenever the prefix index > 0 (i.e., a non‑empty prefix has been matched); stop exploring when the prefix is fully matched or when no outgoing edge matches the next character
Use a visited bitmask or boolean array to enforce simple‑path constraint (no vertex revisited in the current recursion)
Overall worst‑case time O(V + E · L) where L is query length, but pruning by mismatched labels often reduces it; space O(V) recursion stack
Edge cases: repeated characters in the query, self‑loops, disconnected graph, and queries longer than any possible simple path

records.text: Players with fixed rankings. Description: N players and directed match results; return the players whose rank is fully determined by transitive wins and losses; transitive closure or bitsets, plus the correctness argument.
key_points: Build the directed graph of match results; compute transitive closure using Floyd‑Warshall for small N or bitset‑based BFS for larger N (O(N³) vs O(N · (E / word)))
A player’s rank is fully determined when the number of players it can reach (wins) plus the number that can reach it (losses) equals N – 1
Collect all such players; they are exactly the nodes whose relative order is known with respect to every other node
Complexity: O(N³) time and O(N²) space for Floyd‑Warshall; with bitsets, O(N · (E / 64)) time, O(N²/64) space
Edge cases: disconnected components, duplicate match records, and cycles (which are impossible in a strict win‑loss hierarchy but must be handled gracefully)

records.text: Rectangle increments on a grid. Description: Apply many inclusive rectangle +1 updates to an n x n grid and return final counts per cell; 2D difference array then prefix sums.
key_points: Use a 2‑D difference array diff[n+1][n+1]; for each rectangle (x1,y1,x2,y2) do: diff[x1][y1]++, diff[x2+1][y1]--, diff[x1][y2+1]--, diff[x2+1][y2+1]++
After all updates, compute the prefix sum first along rows then along columns to obtain the final grid values
Time complexity: O(K + n²) where K is number of rectangles; space O(n²) for the diff array and result grid
Works for inclusive coordinates; careful with index bounds (use n+1 size to avoid overflow)
Edge cases: rectangles of zero area, updates that touch the grid border, and large K requiring 64‑bit counters

records.text: Three path tasks on a weighted binary grid. Description: Top-to-bottom reachability, deterministic enumeration of simple paths, then minimum-cost weighted path on a blocked grid (BFS, backtracking, Dijkstra).
key_points: Task 1 – Reachability: BFS/DFS from every top‑row cell through allowed moves (down, left, right) respecting blocked cells; stop when any bottom‑row cell is reached
Task 2 – Enumerate all simple top‑to‑bottom paths deterministically: backtrack with a visited set, always exploring moves in a fixed order (e.g., left, down, right) to guarantee a unique ordering
Task 3 – Minimum‑cost path on the same grid with weighted cells: Dijkstra’s algorithm (or 0‑1 BFS if weights are 0/1) on the graph of free cells, using a priority queue keyed by accumulated cost
Overall complexities: reachability O(V + E), enumeration exponential in worst case (but required by problem), Dijkstra O(V log V + E)
Edge cases: completely blocked start or end, multiple equally‑cost paths, and handling of large weight sums (use 64‑bit integers)
